subject: Cognitive Science
title: Overconfidence
description: A quick, practical guide to Overconfidence.

hook.text: Ask people: are you an above-average driver? About 80% say yes. Mathematically, they can't all be right.

buildup.text: Overconfidence is one of the most reliable findings in judgment research. It appears in every culture and profession.

discovery.text: It comes in three forms: overestimating your ability, your knowledge, and your precision of forecasts.

twist.text: Experts are often more overconfident than novices. Greater knowledge inflates certainty faster than accuracy.

climax.text: A calibration study found that when doctors were 90% sure of a diagnosis, they were right only 50% of the time.

details.summary: People systematically overestimate the accuracy of their knowledge and predictions. Confidence regularly exceeds accuracy by wide margins. Overconfidence is strongest for difficult questions and is remarkably resistant to training.
details.whyItMatters: Overconfidence is one of the most pervasive biases. It causes wars, market bubbles, planning failures, and bad forecasts because people believe they know more than they do.
takeaways: Confidence consistently exceeds accuracy across domains
Overconfidence is strongest for hard questions
It drives planning fallacies and excessive risk-taking

faq.question: How is overconfidence measured?
faq.answer: Researchers ask people to answer questions and rate their confidence. When people say they are 90 percent sure, they are correct only about 75 percent of the time. This miscalibration between confidence and accuracy is the core measure of overconfidence.

faq.question: Are experts immune to overconfidence?
faq.answer: No. Experts are often more overconfident than novices because their deep knowledge creates an illusion of predictive ability. Weather forecasters and bridge players are well-calibrated because they receive immediate feedback. Doctors, lawyers, and analysts typically show significant overconfidence.
